item.title: Does the Neuroslop Enrichment Real?
item.description:
Programming Language with unique grammar resembling TCL and Conventional Commits Designed by me coded with ChatGPT after accidental prompt

delegate syntax; retain responsibility.

I share 0.1 version with hello.su first program in it

Perhaps it evolves fast to something big No promises or insight unfortunately It's 3 in 1 now actually cross-platform shell + widget library programming language + scripts packages and OS + coding agent

.su file extension means "script user" not that you think

The language/toolchain uses three file extensions: .su is USSR source, .ua is textual UUASM (USSR Ukraine assembler), and .ru is the intended final VM binary bytecode. The CLI runs all three; .uuasm is retained as a compatibility suffix for assembler source. ussr -c script.su [out.ru] compiles without running, and ussr out.ru runs the result (format: docs/RU_BYTECODE_FORMAT.md).

#ЗДОРОВО МОРЯЧОК emerge(report): "K-152" print(aye): "BOOM!"

The actual list of epithets are:

General Purpose Scripted Multi-paradigm Interpreted Object oriented Open source Free Dynamically typed Shell Preprocessed Imperative Functional Self-referencing Partially AI designed Command Virtually executed Portable Multiplatform

The language is deliberately designed for working with low-quality code en masse with zero equipment You can shout it commands without a pencil standing on construction site fab or in military or city crowd and be understood

Because of AI development we achieved near impossible performance USSR interpreter written in USSR russia.su is up in less than a man month there are even own vi clone Mbl.su (vi->wi->mi->Mbl quality is mediocre but nobody cares the whole thing is running forward like a steam engine now it's all about quantity now how much tests lines of code rosetta tasks interpreted commands gigabytes and other statistical parameters you can imagine

The project uses real existing geographical toponyms or cultural significant objects to name it's scripts e.g. tula.su - 2D CAD ural.su - package manager ukraine.su - httpd daemon and framework tver.su - file manager russia.su - bootstrapped interpreter petersburg.su - gui library kiev.su - main USSR configuration file etc few exceptions are Mbl.su - text editor and no-name std library with shared functions package called library install.su - Moscow kernel installer and top level packages fonts tests docs highlight

Newer subprojects (each has a box.uno in src/<name>/; all of them have code now: the second wave is finished):

dubna.su - PostgreSQL client: protocol 3.0, TLS, SCRAM-SHA-256, parameterised queries (working: src/dubna) omsk.su - image thumbnails: PNG and baseline JPEG in, a 200x200 JPEG out, in pure USSR (working: src/omsk) kgb.su - Knowledge Giga Base, fact-oriented Markdown knowledge base: folders are objects and categories (working: src/kgb) klin.su - GUI calculator, programmer, scientific and casual in one (working: src/klin) kremlin.su - GUI desktop manager, a full-screen desktop on ~/kremlin (working: src/kremlin) novgorod.su - anonymous HTTPS image forum for programmers with lightweight markup (working: src/novgorod) ryazan.su - secure socket library: TLS and HTTPS on Schannel or OpenSSL (working: src/ryazan; ukraine.su serves HTTPS and prompt(_): reaches AI providers through it) siberia.su - GUI spreadsheet: formulas, flat ODF (.fods) and CSV (working: src/siberia) novosibirsk.su - GUI document editor with system fonts, split from Siberia: flat ODF text (.fodt) and .txt (working: src/novosibirsk) Mbltishi.su - the desktop's terminal: the USSR shell in a Petersburg window on Moscow, started from Kremlin (working: src/Mbltishi) moscow.su - amd64 kernel: a NASM two-stage boot loader starts a NASM USSR runtime (a .ru VM on bare metal) that runs moscow.ru, which mounts a Belarus root file system and runs russia.su (the self-hosted interpreter) as its shell with kernel commands like ls():, cat():, run(): and install():; a terminal console (raw keys, ANSI on VGA) that runs the Mbl editor from its source; an e1000 driver and its own TCP/IP stack (DHCP, ARP, ICMP, TCP) behind the Murmansk firewall that serve Novgorod over HTTP and, with BearSSL loaded as a C library, HTTPS; windows: Petersburg in /lib/gui.so on a software OpenGL and a GLFW of its own on the VGA framebuffer, so Kremlin, Mbltishi and Tver run on it, and an installed system boots into the desktop; tasks: spawn runs programs side by side, each in an address space of its own (page tables, demand paging, TLSF heaps), switched by the timer; boots from the Belarus install disk, tested in QEMU (working: src/moscow) belarus.su - the USSR file system: inodes whose block maps are B+ trees from file block index to disk LBA, directories as files of entries; mkfs, ls, put, cat, fsck on disks and images, and Moscow's root (working: src/belarus) murmansk.su - the firewall of Moscow's network stack: ordered allow/deny rules and policies, stateful, rules in /etc/murmansk.rules, fw(_): (working: src/murmansk) install.su - the USSR installer: install(_): in Moscow asks about the disk and partitions, makes a Belarus partition with Stalin and copies USSR onto a virtual disk that then boots (working: src/moscow/install.su) stalin.su - partition editor: lists HDD/SSD/flash devices, edits GPT and MBR tables, recognises ext4, NTFS, UFS, FFS2 and Belarus (working: src/stalin) usa.su - C compiler written in USSR: C99 in, .ru bytecode out, with its own C library; builds pikchr, lemon and tpm (working: src/usa) sochi.su - Preferans for three by the Sochi rules, peer to peer over UDP with LAN discovery and chat (working: src/sochi) lenin.su - the brain center: refines a prompt, spins it through a centrifuge of AI models, measures the answers with your test and extracts the best (working: src/lenin)

Moscow, the amd64 kernel, booting in QEMU with russia.su as its shell:

The ROUND stack is the project's mainline: Ryazan (TLS) under Ukraine (HTTP) under Novgorod (the forum), with Omsk (image thumbnails) making Novgorod's 200x200 previews and Dubna (the PostgreSQL client) under Novgorod's --db.

ussr src/novgorod/novgorod.su # Novgorod on https://localhost:8443/ ussr src/novgorod/novgorod.su --db "postgres://forum:secret@localhost/forum" $include "ural.su" instsall(code): "ukraine russia"

or(if you prefer classic shell)

ural install ukraine russia

USSR is a bug-ridden project critical simple system crippling bugs may appear RANDOMLY in any time any place AI won't help much too big context Examples: it can't print negative numbers else branches is broken e.t.c

USSR is a neuroslopware it's created entirely by prompting an AI followed by enrichment and refining results with the next AI "centrifuge"

Desktop applications run straight from their sources with a GLFW-enabled build:

ussr src/tver/tver.su [directory] # Tver, two-panel file manager ussr src/tula/tula.su [drawing.dxf] # Tula, 2D CAD and DXF viewer ussr src/klin/klin.su [sci|prog] # Klin, calculator ussr src/kremlin/kremlin.su [--window] # Kremlin, desktop on ~/kremlin

KGB, the knowledge base, runs in the terminal:

ussr src/kgb/kgb.su init zoo ussr src/kgb/kgb.su --kb zoo add animals/mammals/cat legs: 4 ussr src/kgb/kgb.su --kb zoo where "legs>2"

Stalin, the partition editor, too; with no command it lists the storage devices. Raw disks (\\.\PhysicalDrive1, /dev/sdb) need administrator rights and --yes; an image file needs neither:

ussr src/stalin/stalin.su ussr src/stalin/stalin.su mkimg disk.img 20M ussr src/stalin/stalin.su init disk.img gpt ussr src/stalin/stalin.su add disk.img --size 8M --type ext4 --name root ussr src/stalin/stalin.su show disk.img

Sochi, three-player Preferans by the Sochi rules: the first copy hosts the table, the others find it on the LAN (UDP port 33333) or join it by address, and the three chat while they play:

ussr src/sochi/sochi.su # nickname, then the tables on the LAN ussr src/sochi/sochi.su host --bots 2 # a table with two bots ussr src/sochi/sochi.su join 192.168.1.20 # a table across the network

usa, the C compiler, closes the circle: C goes in, .ru bytecode comes out and runs on the same VM as everything else:

ussr src/usa/usa.su hello.c # writes hello.ru ussr hello.ru

Lenin is the neuroslop code enrichment and refining AI agent (working: src/lenin, see its README).

USSR itself is made by prompting an AI and refining the results with the next AI "centrifuge" by hand. Lenin is that process as a program. Practice what you preach: if enriched neuroslop is better than classical software then the enrichment has to be a tool and it has to show it.

ussr src/lenin/lenin.su --models models.conf --dir out --cycles 3 \ --criteria speed --test "python test.py {file}" --ext .py "what you want"

You give it:

the prompt the centrifuge models, from different developers (the API keys stay in environment variables, the file only names them) the optimization criteria (speed, size) the working directory the generation cycles repeat count a test that says whether an answer works, and if you have one a classic solution to measure against

You get the best of what the models gave, by your test:

It refines the prompt so it precisely reflects things in reality It gives the refined prompt to the centrifuge models They work on it for the given number of cycles, each cycle (or with --method chain each centrifuge, one after another) seeing the best answer so far and how it measured It runs every answer through your test and extracts the one that passes and is best by your criteria

What it does and does not show:

An answer that fails the test cannot win. That part is measured, not an opinion of a model Best means best by the test you wrote. With a weak test the winner is whatever gets past it: given a canned answer assert 2+3==5 to a task of printing a sum, and a test that only looked at the exit status, Lenin picks it for its size. Without a test the models only vote, and the report says nothing was run With a baseline, the report says whether the winner beat that classic solution on that one task Whether this adds up to better than classical software is not shown yet. So far Lenin has run against canned models only, to test Lenin itself. src/lenin/examples/wordcount is the first benchmark, waiting for real models and real keys

The project now has three main tracks, with the Moscow OS kernel underneath (Lenin runs on a hosted ussr for now: on Moscow it has no TLS to reach a model):

The ROUND stack forum: Ryazan, Ukraine, Novgorod, Omsk and Dubna The Kremlin GUI desktop and its apps, with the USSR shell Lenin, the neuroslop code enrichment and refining AI agent

With usa the second wave is done and USSR is complete. Its programs:

ussr/ussr.exe - the USSR programming language and shell russia.su - bootstrapped USSR interpreter, written in USSR moscow.su - amd64 kernel: the NASM USSR runtime runs russia.su as its shell on a Belarus root (sh src/moscow/build.sh) lenin.su - the USSR brain center neuroslop enrichment agent ukraine.su - HTTP server and web framework kiev.su - the USSR startup configuration file belarus.su - the USSR file system: per-file B+ tree block maps library (src/libs) - the USSR standard library: io, math, bytes, strings, vectors ural.su - USSR package manager petersburg - OpenGL GUI widgets, dialogs, events and layout Mbl.su - vi-like console text editor Mbltishi.su - terminal window of the desktop (on Moscow) tver.su - GUI two-panel file manager tula.su - GUI 2D CAD with DXF klin.su - GUI calculator: casual, scientific and programmer modes ryazan.su - TLS and HTTPS on Schannel or OpenSSL kremlin.su - GUI full-screen desktop on ~/kremlin novgorod.su - anonymous HTTPS image forum (ROUND stack) dubna.su - PostgreSQL client (ROUND stack) omsk.su - image thumbnails: PNG and baseline JPEG in pure USSR (ROUND stack) siberia.su - GUI spreadsheet novosibirsk.su - GUI document editor kgb.su - Knowledge Giga Base, fact-oriented Markdown knowledge base stalin.su - GPT/MBR partition editor sochi.su - three-player Preferans over UDP usa.su - C compiler to .ru bytecode install.su - the moscow OS installer: install(_): puts USSR on a disk of its own

item.title: App Store 2026 in numbers: AI, pricing, abandoned apps
item.description:
Research · Data as of November 6, 2026

App Store 2026 in numbers

We looked at 178,637 apps that appeared in the App Store top charts of 173 countries and regions since October 9, 2026. Here are the answers to five questions.

Key findings About 1 in 10 apps in the charts mention AI in their store listing (9.8%); in Graphics & Design it is 43%. Apps that sell in-app purchases or subscriptions are 3 times as likely to mention AI as plain free apps (19.9% vs 6.6%). 26.7% of free-to-download apps sell in-app purchases or subscriptions; most in Graphics & Design (60.2%), fewest in Shopping (11.5%). 20.3% of apps in the charts have not been updated for a year or more; 9.8% for over three years. In 1-2 star reviews the most common complaint is subscription & price (12.7%), ahead of bugs & broken features (10.9%) and login & account (10%). 1. How many apps talk about AI

17,456 apps (9.8%) mention AI, GPT, machine learning, generative or chatbot in their name or the start of their description. They cluster in Graphics & Design, Photo & Video and Developer Tools. Ratings barely differ: among apps with at least 50 ratings, those mentioning AI average 4.49 stars and the rest 4.4.

Show the numbers Category Apps Share Graphics & Design 2,644 43.0% Photo & Video 5,073 23.4% Developer Tools 2,183 22.1% Productivity 7,671 16.9% Health & Fitness 9,695 15.2% Education 15,799 12.9% Reference 5,867 11.9% Lifestyle 8,676 11.1% Music 4,399 10.8% Entertainment 7,167 9.1% Social Networking 4,332 9.0% Sports 8,704 8.8% Utilities 7,795 8.6% Finance 11,266 7.7% Business 9,899 7.5% Medical 7,034 7.3% Books 5,626 6.6% News 6,979 6.1% Weather 2,942 5.2% Food & Drink 9,202 4.6% Games 7,325 4.5% Shopping 7,234 3.2% Travel 6,682 3.2% Navigation 5,400 2.6%
2. How free apps make money

Of 164,056 free-to-download apps, 26.7% say in their description that they offer in-app purchases, a subscription, a trial or a Pro unlock. Graphics & Design and Photo & Video lead; Shopping and News come last; many of those are apps of businesses that most likely earn their money outside the app.

Show the numbers Category Apps Share Graphics & Design 2,583 60.2% Photo & Video 3,462 56.1% Games 5,425 44.0% Music 4,118 40.5% Productivity 5,542 40.1% Health & Fitness 8,227 39.8% Developer Tools 2,129 34.3% Entertainment 5,840 33.2% Utilities 7,253 33.1% Social Networking 4,074 31.3% Weather 2,903 31.1% Reference 5,790 29.6% Lifestyle 8,401 29.4% Education 12,669 27.2% Sports 8,550 26.5% Navigation 5,323 24.5% Finance 10,465 23.4% Books 5,573 21.2% Medical 6,979 18.0% Travel 6,612 16.4% Business 9,795 16.2% Food & Drink 9,148 13.8% News 6,950 13.5% Shopping 7,223 11.5%
3. How much of the charts independent developers hold

By our definition (see the notes below), 67.3% of apps in the charts come from independent developers. Their ratings match the larger publishers': 4.41 against 4.41 stars for apps with at least 50 ratings. The share is highest in Developer Tools, Sports and Navigation and lowest in Games.

Show the numbers Category Apps Share Developer Tools 2,183 76.5% Sports 8,704 74.7% Navigation 5,400 74.4% Weather 2,942 73.7% Productivity 7,671 72.0% Travel 6,682 71.6% Graphics & Design 2,644 71.5% Health & Fitness 9,695 70.6% Shopping 7,234 69.7% Medical 7,034 69.2% Lifestyle 8,676 68.8% Food & Drink 9,202 67.9% Reference 5,867 67.6% Utilities 7,795 66.9% Music 4,399 66.8% Education 15,799 66.7% Entertainment 7,167 66.7% Business 9,899 65.9% Social Networking 4,332 65.9% Photo & Video 5,073 64.5% Books 5,626 64.4% Finance 11,266 62.0% News 6,979 60.4% Games 7,325 59.9%
4. How many apps are no longer maintained

70.9% of apps in the charts were updated in the last six months, yet 20.3% have gone a year or more without an update and 9.8% more than three years. Books, Reference and News have the most apps left alone; Finance the fewest (10.9%).

Show the numbers Category Apps Share Books 5,626 36.3% Reference 5,867 33.6% News 6,979 32.5% Medical 7,034 26.4% Music 4,399 26.3% Weather 2,942 25.2% Entertainment 7,167 25.1% Education 15,799 24.2% Photo & Video 5,073 24.1% Navigation 5,400 22.2% Graphics & Design 2,644 20.9% Developer Tools 2,183 20.0% Food & Drink 9,202 19.2% Social Networking 4,332 18.2% Lifestyle 8,676 17.7% Productivity 7,671 17.7% Utilities 7,795 17.1% Health & Fitness 9,695 17.0% Business 9,899 16.0% Games 7,325 15.4% Shopping 7,234 14.9% Sports 8,704 14.3% Travel 6,682 13.3% Finance 11,266 10.9%
5. What bad reviews complain about

We read 165,735 US App Store reviews of 3,912 apps. Among 1-2 star reviews, 12.7% complain about subscription & price, 10.9% about bugs & broken features and 10% about login & account. One review can fall under several themes.

Next edition

We will refresh this report every quarter. From the next edition it will show change over time: which apps moved to subscriptions, how fast the AI share grows, and whether abandoned apps come back.

How to read these numbers Scope: 178,637 iPhone, iPad and Mac apps that appeared in an App Store top chart since October 9, 2026. In 12 large markets that means the overall and category charts for free, paid and top grossing apps; elsewhere the overall free chart. Apps never seen in a chart are left out. Categories: the app's primary App Store category, with names in other languages merged. Categories with fewer than 1,500 apps have no row of their own. Mentions AI: the name or the first 1,500 characters of the description contain AI, GPT, artificial intelligence, machine learning, generative, LLM or chatbot. It shows the app markets itself with AI, not that its features depend on it. Sells in-app purchases or subscriptions: free to download, and the description mentions a subscription, in-app purchase, premium, trial, unlock, Pro or a monthly or yearly price. Apps that say nothing may still sell something, so this share is on the low side. Independent developer: at most 5 of the developer's apps seen in the charts, no app with 30,000 ratings or more, and a seller name that does not read as a company (Inc, Corp, GmbH and the like). We only see apps that charted, so this share may run high. Last update: the release date of the current version on the US App Store. Reviews: recent public reviews on the US App Store. Themes come from keywords (for example subscription, ads, crash); shares are of 1-2 star reviews, except feature requests, which are of all reviews. Recent reviews lean negative, so we do not publish the overall share of bad reviews. Ratings: only apps with at least 50 ratings count. Cite and download

The charts and data are free to use, commercial use included (CC BY 4.0). Please credit “Obelisk Club” and link to this page.

Suggested citation

Obelisk Club, “App Store 2026 in numbers”, November 6, 2026, https://obelisk.club/research/app-store-2026

About the bubbles and this research sample

Who is included: employers with more than 1,000 worldwide employees in at least one sourced year and a documented Bay Area workplace. All records includes unresolved and outside-tech cases; use the scope and industry filters to narrow the sample.

Reading the map: bubbles show workplaces or approximate city presence, not employee totals. Hollow bubbles are city-level records; cluster numbers count distinct employers. Click a bubble for dated evidence and sources. The dashed rectangle marks the study extent, not complete coverage.

Gaps are not closures: supported presence intervals remain visible; short carry-forwards are labeled estimated. Older observations appear only with “Show last-known locations,” and remain unverified. Confirmed closures or departures suppress the affected locations. All recorded years combines observations from different dates.

Navigation: drag to pan; use +/− or Ctrl+scroll to zoom. Keyboard: arrows, +/− and Home. The timeline advances in five-year steps; Latest shows 2026. Roads and boundaries are US Census 2024 geography, not historical reconstructions. City positions remain approximate at every zoom.

San Francisco · government employment statistics

San Francisco tech employment share

High-tech industry jobs as a percentage of all QCEW-covered jobs in San Francisco County. Census's high-tech industry definition, applied to BLS county data; this is a separate calculation from the employer map.

▲ Published minimum: the true share may be higher. ● Complete published basket. Lines connect annual published values within each industry definition, not estimates of missing employment. Gaps and definition changes break the line.

1960–1989 has no comparable series here; 2026 has no full-year observation. The 2022 industry-code change alters the basket, so values across that boundary are not directly comparable. Missing industry cells can change the published minimum without employment actually changing.

Definition, industry codes and sources

Jobs are counted at workplaces, not by where workers live. QCEW excludes many self-employed workers and is not a count of all people working. San Francisco County is the fixed statistical unit. No employer-size cutoff applies.
